synopsis: Across Brazil, Chile, Peru, India, China and Japan, the booklet found general mining or machinery safety obligations but no dedicated rule with numeric tests for off-road automatic braking; for the South American findings, “not found” explicitly does not mean “not required” [f15576, f15586]. South America has no continent-wide machinery regime: Brazil uses NR-22 and NR-12, Chile DS 132, and Peru DS 024-2016-EM; Brazil's NR-22 was last modified on 29 January 2026, while Chile's DS 132 was promulgated in 2002, published in 2004 and consolidated to 2024 [f2285, f2130, f2131, f2132, f2286, f15581]. India's DGMS circular dated 21 August 2024 calls for proximity-warning or anti-collision devices on wheeled trackless machinery in opencast coal mines, a 2025 circular addresses fail-safe braking before tipper deployment, and a cited circular sets 30 km/h; these details have low confidence because only secondary summaries were reviewed, and no standardised national interaction-test matrix was found [f2302, f2303, f2304, f2307, f2453]. China's reported underground requirement is at least 50 m between rubber-tyred vehicles travelling in the same direction, but the regulation itself was not reviewed, and relevant GB/GB/T adoptions were not established [f2298, f2299, f2198]. No dedicated Japanese off-road automatic-braking rule was found, general safety provisions should not be interpreted as such a mandate, and JARI is a weather-test facility rather than a regulator [f2308, f2309, f15594]. Planning should therefore retain project acceptance criteria grounded in general obligations and configurable site-specific expectations, while recognising unresolved Chilean regulator guidance and uncertainty in the Indian and Chinese evidence [f15596, f15597, f2293, f2307, f2299].
